One of the theories about how a former Apple employee obtained confidential files after leaving the company to join OpenAI has been debunked by a court filing.

There had been speculation that the former employee may have obtained the documents without realising due to chaotic iCloud account arrangements for Apple staff — but Apple says that's not the case...

A quick recap

Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI last month, accusing the company of stealing trade secrets related to a hardware project. One key part of the allegations involves a former Apple employee named Chang Liu, who subsequently moved to OpenAI. Here's a short timeline of events:

  • July 10: Apple files lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing former Apple employee of systematically stealing Apple's trade secrets to benefit OpenAI's future hardware development
  • July 10: OpenAI issues brief denial in response
  • July 14: OpenAI updates response, stating it has not seen any evidence supporting Apple's allegations
  • August 3: OpenAI publishes blog post attacking Apple's lawsuit
  • August 4: Apple applies for temporary injunction to avoid "irreparable harm"

The iCloud chaos

OpenAI said that a flaw in Apple's information security meant the former employee retained "unnecessary" access to confidential files after leaving the company.

Earlier, The Information published a report suggesting the claim was related to chaotic iCloud arrangements.

The report said that while Apple removes former employees' access to company-managed iCloud folders, many files had likely been shared to Apple employees' personal accounts — and these former employees not only retained access to those files after leaving, but might even receive push updates for them.

In other words, former employees could receive push updates for confidential files on their personal devices, without having done anything wrong themselves.

Apple says this isn't the case

However, John Gruber of Daring Fireball has noted that Apple explicitly stated in its court filing that the files in question were not stored on iCloud.

Gruber suggests it's highly likely the files involved Box, a cloud storage service widely used inside Apple.

9to5Mac's take

Right now everything is still very much in the he-said-she-said stage. We need to wait for the court to adjudicate the actual case before we can separate fact from fiction.

However, this issue of chaotic iCloud arrangements does seem to have been implicitly acknowledged by Apple to some extent. The arrangement appears to have been intended to avoid Apple employees needing to carry both a personal and a work iPhone. While understandable, it does seem to represent a significant security loophole.
